source_review.notes: Checked ACM-linked, SIAM, Springer, author, DBLP, textbook-publisher, and official OpenMP records for Brent simulation, Graham scheduling, Cilk, randomized work stealing, multiprogrammed scheduling, work/span exposition, task dependences, and parallel algorithm design. OpenMP behavior is explicitly tied to version 5.2 rather than described as an unversioned current default. No latest-runtime, processor-performance, or universal scalability claim is made.

evidence: Checked computation DAG, strand weight, work, span, processor runtime, earliest finish, critical path, parallelism, speedup, efficiency, ready set, and bandwidth notation before use.
Checked ideal/measured, weighted/unit, semantic/scheduler/resource, expected/worst-case, fully-strict/arbitrary, real/floating, and lower/upper-bound qualifiers plus balanced GitHub math delimiters.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Work, serial wall time, useful work, work inflation, span, width, and processor utilization remain distinct quantities.

evidence: Recomputed all task costs, earliest finishes, schedule intervals, lower bounds, parallelism, speedup, efficiency, grain-overhead ratios, work-stealing scales, bandwidth interpretation, and floating-order cases.
Enumerated all 64 forward-edge DAGs on four labeled vertices and checked legal greedy schedules for one, two, and four processors: 192 schedule/model combinations.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Operation counts and hypothetical timings are declared model inputs, not wall-clock benchmarks.

evidence: Re-derived work and span laws, combined lower bound, maximum speedup bound, topological longest-path recurrence, and Brent-style work-plus-depth charging.
Re-derived schedule legality, critical-path reconstruction, work-inflation distinction, bandwidth lower-bound form, and why real associativity does not imply floating reproducibility.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: Published greedy and work-stealing upper bounds remain attached to their precise scheduling and computation models.

evidence: Checked empty and single-strand graphs, chains, antichains, diamonds, combs, high fan-in/out, equal critical paths, skewed weights, cycles, unknown dependencies, and insufficient processors.

Checked missing and excessive edges, tiny grains, barriers, hot atomics, false sharing, NUMA, bandwidth saturation, oversubscription, exceptions, side effects, floating exceptional behavior, hostile schedules, and fallback.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Acyclicity and schedule legality are not treated as proof of complete semantic dependence or optimality.

evidence: Checked acyclicity, resolved dependency identity, exactly-once strand execution, predecessor completion, processor nonoverlap, weight-model consistency, result equivalence, and theorem-assumption invariants.
All 192 enumerated schedules respected every edge and processor capacity, met work/span lower bounds, and remained within a Brent-style work-plus-span ceiling.
invariant_checking.notes: Independent static interval checks support every finite schedule trace, not merely its makespan.

evidence: Reviewed processor-capacity and critical-path lower bounds separately, then their speedup consequences and finite-processor simulation argument.
Reviewed semantic dependency completeness, topological recurrence, greedy schedule validation, fully strict work-stealing scope, numerical equivalence, and performance attribution.
proof_review.notes: The executable proves a deterministic ideal list schedule only; it does not implement or prove a concurrent runtime.

evidence: Audited theorem, principle, proof, lower bound, upper bound, asymptotic, expected, ideal, measured, critical, optimal, legal, empirical, and operational language.
Separated computation semantics, abstract schedule, scheduler heuristic, runtime mechanism, hardware resource, measurement, numerical policy, and production judgment.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: No expected work-stealing result, greedy bound, or abstract work/span law is presented as an exact hardware runtime equation.

evidence: The CPython 3.14.4 snippet exited zero with exact topology, work, span, lower bound, seven task intervals, and makespan on macOS 13.7.8 x86_64.
Independent enumeration checked 192 unit-DAG schedules and all weighted exercise arithmetic.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: Execution supports the declared bounded ideal model only; it does not establish thread safety, optimal scheduling in general, work-stealing bounds, memory locality, bandwidth, reproducibility, security, or production performance.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed computation-DAG construction, work, span, critical paths, lower and upper bounds, greedy schedules, semantic dependencies, work stealing, granularity, inflation, hidden resources, numerical semantics, and measurement.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed races, barriers, atomics, queues, steals, task cutoff, locality, false sharing, NUMA, bandwidth, affinity, oversubscription, exceptions, side effects, seeds, benchmarks, sanitizers, schedule fuzzing, telemetry, and safe fallback.

pedagogical_review.notes: The Level-II chapter derives work/span bounds, executes and critiques a complete weighted DAG schedule, connects classic scheduling theory to runtime constraints, supplies ten distinct examples, and ends with five progressive exercises and complete answers.

limitations: Internal source, mathematical, snippet, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical review only; no external academic, parallel-algorithm, runtime, operating-system, architecture, compiler, numerical, genomics, performance, or operational review is claimed. Formal and empirical conclusions remain conditional on DAG completeness, strand weights, processor model, computation structure, scheduler, randomness, granularity, memory hierarchy, numeric semantics, input, compiler, hardware, measurement, and output-equivalence assumptions.
